newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: FEATURE - Hope flickers dimly for poisoned Azeri city.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hope flickers dimly for poisoned Azeri city.

text.p: A noxious odour of chlorine hangs thickly in the air above the hundreds of infant graves gradually disappearing under the tall weeds in Sumgait's cemetery.

Twenty km (13 miles) north of Azerbaijan's capital Baku, the city is a graveyard to the illusion of a thriving Soviet industrial base, and now threatens to stymie those trying to give it a new future as a modern production centre.

Instead of a workers' heaven, a mad rush to industrialise the backward Soviet Union turned Sumgait into a poisoned hell where an extremely intense concentration of factories churned out some of the most toxic substances known to man.
"On some days the smoke was so thick you couldn't even see where you were going. My eyes would start watering as soon as I went outside," said Eldar, a local who used to work in one.
And an astronomical incidence of birth defects bears witness to the long-term effects.

Now, with most factories running at only about a quarter of capacity after a post-Soviet economic slump, dark orange smoke still wafts from some of the rusting plants and a putrid smell of chemicals is palpable everywhere -- but the stench of corruption is almost as pervasive.

Years of coaxing from international bodies have helped prompt the government to try to relaunch Sumgait as a special economic zone but have done little to check the powerful factory bosses who profited from the post-Soviet economic upheaval and now want to derail the project.
"These people are millionaires many times over, and they stand to lose everything if they lose control," said U.N. resident representative Paolo Lembo. "I don't know if we can defeat them."
MASSIVE CONCENTRATION OF FACTORIES WAS UNIQUE

Soviet central planners aimed to make Sumgait Azerbaijan's production hub and jammed 80 percent of the republic's industries into its small radius, driving the population from just 6,000 in 1940 to more than 350,000 by 1985.

"The drive was for industrialisation at all costs. Build, build, build. The factories were put right on top of each other," said Arif Islamzade, chief ecologist of a U.N.-led programme aimed at rebuilding the city.

Inside the plants, workers brewed a toxic soup of pesticides and fertilizers: DDT, superphosphates, chlorine, lindane and even the Soviet equivalent of the defoliant "Agent Orange" used in the Vietnam War.
Islamzade and other medical and environmental experts say this led to a huge rate of health problems and horrible birth defects.
Industrial waste was simply dumped into the ground or pumped out into the nearby Caspian Sea, contaminating drinking water and food grown in local gardens right next to factories.
WORKERS TRADED HEALTH FOR GROCERIES

Plentiful housing -- a rarity in much of the country at the time -- relatively high wages and prized workplace perks such as milk, meat and cheese wooed workers from all corners of the now-defunct Soviet Union.

"People didn't think about what was going on here then. 'The Soviet state needs labourers! Come to work!' they told us. Now the generation that is being born is paying the price," said Khalida Qulieva, Sumgait's head paediatrician, who has the unenviable task of tracking the rate of birth defects.
The frequency of ghastly defects like babies born with half a brain or without spines has declined from the peak years in the 1980's. But it remains higher than in the rest of the country.
One-third of all pregnancies in Sumgait involve complications, far above national and world norms.
"There is no question about the ecological effects of all that went on here. This legacy will probably remain for another two generations," Qulieva said.
Six-year old Elchin Mamedov is a typical example. Born paralysed and suffering from convulsions, he twists limply as his father, Ayub, dresses him in a green sweater.

Ayub says his young nephew suffers from the same condition, as do many other children in the neighbourhood of the family home, a one-storey house near the plant where Ayub worked for several years making chlorine detergent and glues.

"We've been to specialist after specialist but no one can do anything for him," says Ayub, adding that 60 to 70 percent of workers in his factory, most of whom used little or no protective gear, suffered from health problems.

Social and economic woes have added to Sumgait's pollution ills in the wake of Azerbaijan's independence from the Soviet Union. Most people in the city are now effectively unemployed or forced to engage in petty trade to get by.
At one street market old women in traditional headscarves hawk plastic jugs of chlorine bleach scavenged from the industrial area, known locally as the 'dead zone', next to apples and cucumbers.
Many women of child-bearing age do not get a proper diet and the stresses of the country's conflict with neighbouring Armenia are taking their toll, Quliyeva says.
CORRUPTION REMAINS A BLOCK TO CITY'S REVIVAL
When the scale of the Sumgait calamity became known to the outside world, few gave the city much hope for revival.
Some foreign experts, including one IMF official, recommended it be evacuated and its residents resettled.
"People were saying the city was lost. How do you evacuate a city of 350,000 people? Load them up like cattle?" said Lembo.

The slender, intense Italian diplomat led the drive to get the government to make the city as a special economic zone despite resistance by the bosses of Sumgait's state-run factories and what he says is a general atmosphere of corruption.
"The city was sinking, and our first concern was how to rescue it. It wasn't just a novel idea," he told Reuters.

Special tax holidays on profits are planned for investors, along with other incentives. Projects must conform to strict ecological standards and there are proposals for a locally managed clean-up fund to help detoxify the city.
"There is a lot of interest on the part of serious foreign investors. They believe Sumgait can be a good base for production. The infrastructure is there," says Lembo.
But the government seems unable to take a determined stance against the men Lembo calls "corrupt barons" who have got rich on illegal sales of state property.
He blames the same circles for numerous death threats he has received, which prompted the country's interior ministry to assign him a round-the-clock bodyguard.
"It's very bizarre. They have the potential to make it work, but they don't have enough enthusiasm," he said.
"This is Sumgait's last chance and its only hope. Without investment the place will completely collapse."
